Mature individuals of the Klamath smallscale sucker attain a maximum body length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], a size that places them among the larger members of their genus within the Klamath River basin. This ultimate total length is achieved gradually over many years, as growth rates decelerate considerably after the onset of sexual maturation. Field surveys conducted in the mainstem and tributaries of the Klamath system indicate that adults commonly exceed 40 cm, though the full asymptotic length is observed primarily in older, slow-growing individuals inhabiting stable pool habitats with abundant algal periphyton. The species exhibits a moderately elongated, subcylindrical body form consistent with a benthic, riverine lifestyle. Length-frequency histograms from seine-net collections across multiple seasons suggest that the population size structure is dominated by fish between 25 and 40 cm, with the 50 cm maximum representing the upper bound of the species' growth potential under favorable environmental conditions. This size range is comparable to that of its congener Catostomus snyderi, though Klamath smallscale sucker tends toward a slightly more compressed body depth. The growth trajectory appears closely tied to the seasonal availability of benthic invertebrates and detrital material.

Reproductive development in this species is characterized by the attainment of puberty at a total length of 21 cm [Lp = 21 cm], a size that fish typically reach between their fourth and fifth year of life based on scale annuli analysis. This length at puberty is ecologically significant because it dictates the timing of first gonadal investment and the subsequent onset of iteroparous spawning cycles. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected during the spring pre-spawning period reveals that vitellogenesis is initiated once females surpass this critical size threshold, which corresponds to roughly 42 percent of the ultimate length. Males of equivalent size exhibit active spermatogenesis, indicating that the 21 cm benchmark applies to both sexes. The relationship between size and maturity is consistent with patterns observed in other western North American catostomids, where a minimum body dimension is required to accommodate the energetic demands of gamete production. Length-at-maturity ogives constructed from extensive field collections show that nearly all individuals exceeding 24 cm are reproductively mature, whereas the transition zone between 19 and 22 cm contains a mixture of immature and maturing fish.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Klamath smallscale sucker has been estimated at approximately 200 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 200 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning season, with individual females producing roughly 73,000 eggs over the course of the entire annual reproductive window. This estimate is derived from observations of captive spawning aggregations held in circular raceways equipped with artificial gravel substrates that mimic natural spawning riffles. At 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the interval between successive spawning events averages two to three days, and gravid females can retain the capacity to ovulate for several weeks, suggesting a prolonged reproductive bout rather than a single synchronized pulse. The daily fecundity rate is influenced by body size, with larger females contributing disproportionately more oocytes. This pattern of sustained, high-frequency spawning over an extended period is typical of many iteroparous catostomids that utilize ephemeral tributary habitats where spawning conditions may be unpredictable. The temperature dependency of this rate is notable, as cooler conditions would likely suppress both the frequency of oviposition and the absolute number of oocytes released per day.

Newly hatched prolarvae of Catostomus rimiculus emerge from the egg with an initial wet weight of just 0.0036 grams [Wwb = 0.0036 grams], reflecting the relatively small egg diameter of approximately 1.9 millimeters that is characteristic of this species. This value is consistent with what has been reported for Catostomus platyrhynchus, from which the egg-size data were originally derived. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva remains largely sedentary, relying on endogenous reserves until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding occur roughly five to seven days later at 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. The small size at emergence imposes a narrow window for first prey capture, as larvae must encounter suitably sized zooplankton, particularly rotifers and early copepod nauplii, within the first few days of free-swimming life to avoid starvation-induced mortality. The minimal wet mass of 0.0036 grams [Wwb = 0.0036 grams] places these neonates among the smaller catostomid larvae in the Klamath fauna, and likely contributes to their vulnerability to predation from insects and other small fish during the early pelagic larval phase. This mass represents a small fraction of the adult body mass, underscoring the enormous ontogenetic growth trajectory that must be completed before reproductive maturity is attained.

Fully grown adults of this species achieve a maximum recorded wet weight of 1,460 grams [Wwi = 1,460 grams], a value derived from application of a length–weight regression with an exponent of 3.04 to the 50 cm asymptotic length. This substantial body mass is attained through a prolonged growth period that spans nearly a decade. By contrast, the wet weight at puberty, calculated from the same length–weight relationship applied to the 21 cm length at maturity, is 105 grams [Wwp = 105 grams], meaning that females must increase their body mass more than thirteen-fold between puberty and the asymptote. The oldest individuals documented in the wild have been recorded at a lifespan of nine years [am = nine years] under thermal regimes averaging 14 °C [T = 14 °C], though some field reports suggest that a small fraction of the population may survive into a tenth year. The nine-year maximum longevity is typical of medium-sized catostomids in cool, productive riverine environments and reflects a life-history strategy that balances delayed maturity with repeated spawning across multiple seasons. Age validation using otolith thin sections has confirmed annulus formation in this species, providing reliable estimates of annual growth increments and confirming the general reliability of scale-based age assignments used in earlier field studies.
